It may appear that way, and until a grand unified theory which fully models the behavior of the universe is established there will continue to be the appearance of numerous gaps in our knowledge of it. The fact of the situation is, that over the past few centuries humanity has achieved a very good understanding of the fundamental behaviors of the universe. An understanding which is not immediately and entirely invalidated because of a phenomena which has yet to be explained.

While Newtonian mechanics are not the end all be all to gravity, they sufficiently explain the behavior of objects subjected to it. Despite the importance and need of relativistic or quantum physics to the greater understanding of human knowledge of the universe, we do not need them explicitly stated and integrated into our models to be able to make accurate predictions within reason.

That said, gravity is an acceleration dependent on the amount of mass present, while force is the reaction between object(s) with mass while under some acceleration (Force = Mass*Acceleration). For example a 1 kg object under 9.81 m/s/s of gravitic acceleration would apply a force of 9.81 Newtons to the ground whilst sitting on the ground.

Acceleration, is merely the rate at which the velocity of an object changes with respect to time. We tend to distinguish gravity because (while it is an acceleration adhering to the previously defined term) its cause is not a deliberate act of adding energy to a system by mechanical means to alter velocity, but the resultant interaction of space and mass.

Mass (of sufficient scale) is capable of distorting euclidean space (typical three dimensional Cartesian space) around it. How it achieves this is a matter of debate and subject to exhaustive discussion. Needless to say, it doesn't really matter how it achieves this (since this isn't a rigorous explanation), it is sufficient to understand that it does and that there may be more to consider in the future. This spatial distortion is verified by both the time differential between terrestrial clocks (sidereal time) and clocks on objects in orbit; as well as by the gravitational lensing effect which massive objects placed in front of stellar (star) light sources produce.

The distortion of space and time, results in the acceleration of objects towards one another and can be construed as the description of the behavior of how objects fall towards one another. Yes.

If gravity is a constant force with the potential to create energy (watermills for example), what is the source of this endless energy?

Gravity doesn't create energy, an object possesses potential energy when gravity is applied to it (and all objects with mass in the universe have a potential energy with one another). That potential energy becomes kinetic energy as the object's velocity increases and their subsequent distance from one another decreases (as they fall towards each other). That potential energy will eventually be reduced to a limit as the object comes to rest against another mass (such as the surface of the Earth) as it can no longer translate through space. So the energy isn't, endless, all energy has a fundamental limit and this limit is conserved across the entirety of the system (thermodynamics).

Watermills derive energy from the flow of water (generally considered to be down hill). So gravity is applied to water (uphill), and due to the mass of water potential energy exists. The water moves down hill as that potential energy is converted to kinetic energy through the movement of water. The water applies energy to the watermill, which then performs work for, whatever purpose. The water will ultimately end up in the ocean, at which point (for the sake of this example) it will no longer posess energy that can be utilized. If there was only a set amount of water uphill, then eventually that resource would be fully exploited and could no longer be used. Fortunately the water cycle exists, so water is evaporated off oceans by sunlight, and returns to land via rainfall, so this situation doesn't occur.

Of course this is a very simplified example and there is a lot going on which may or may not be readily apparent. To gain a fuller understanding of what's going on, 12th grade to college level physics based courses are a good start (physics, optics, thermodynamics, vector mechanics, and all that calculus).
